method: Source-backed process chemistry and stability observations. Published ranges/guides remain factual fields; game risk effects are separately marked derived and must not be presented as analytical diagnoses.

facts: YAN combines ammonium nitrogen and alpha-amino nitrogen available to yeast.
Nitrogen demand depends on yeast strain, sugar, temperature and aeration; one YAN target is not universal.
Low YAN is associated with growth-phase hydrogen sulfide risk, but H2S response to nitrogen addition depends on yeast strain and must conditions.
Nitrogen supplementation can reduce some slow/stuck fermentation and reduction risks but is not a deterministic cure.
Late fermentation H2S can occur after yeast growth has largely ceased and may not respond to DAP in the same way as growth-associated H2S.
Some late H2S cases can respond to aeration or vitamin status; mechanism and response are context dependent.
Higher red fermentation temperature increases fermentation and extraction rates.
Must temperature can materially influence phenolic extraction; higher temperatures can increase seed-derived phenolics.
Very high fermentation temperatures and repeated temperature swings can reduce yeast viability and increase sluggish/stuck fermentation risk.
Volatile acidity is predominantly acetic acid in wine and can become sensorially detrimental well before a universal legal limit is reached.
Acetic acid bacteria use oxygen to oxidize ethanol toward acetic acid.
Ethyl acetate is influenced by yeast strain, fermentation temperature, amino nitrogen, sulfur dioxide, acetic acid bacteria and oxygen exposure.
Brettanomyces can generate volatile phenols including 4-ethylphenol, 4-ethylguaiacol and 4-ethylcatechol.
Brettanomyces is not exclusively a red-wine issue; white wines can be affected.
Mousiness is associated with microbial metabolites including ACTPY, ETPY and ACPY and is often associated with lactic acid bacteria.
Low sulfur dioxide and lower acidity can increase susceptibility; oxygen may enhance expression, but causality is not represented as a simple one-variable rule.
Wine movement before packaging can substantially increase dissolved oxygen.
Inert-gas adjustment can reduce dissolved oxygen before bottling.
Oxygen exposure can indirectly consume free sulfur dioxide during packaging and ageing; the relationship is useful as a risk guide but is not a universal bottle-by-bottle stoichiometric diagnosis.
Closure oxygen transmission and oxygen introduced at packaging influence free sulfur dioxide retention and sensory development.
Closure differences become particularly relevant during bottle ageing and can shift oxidative/reductive expression.
Premature oxidation describes unexpectedly oxidized wine that would otherwise be expected to age longer.
It is multifactorial and can involve oxygen exposure, antioxidant capacity, closure/package oxygen and storage; it cannot be diagnosed from one scalar input.
Oxidation is a major limiting factor in wine ageing capacity, but no single simple assay definitively predicts a wine's ageing capacity.
Wine pH affects microbial stability, sulfur dioxide effectiveness, tartrate equilibrium, red-wine colour, enzyme activity and oxidation/browning behavior.
pH must therefore remain an independent chemical variable rather than being inferred from titratable acidity.
Potassium hydrogen tartrate is the most common crystalline bottle instability.
A wine can differ between current and potential tartrate stability because crystallization inhibitors can change during ageing.
Tartrate precipitation is primarily a physical stability issue and must not automatically be scored as microbial spoilage or sensory deterioration.
